response.task_summary: Predict whether a diabetic inpatient encounter will be followed by hospital readmission, where robust signals should reflect illness burden, prior utilization, glycemic control, and treatment intensity rather than site- or subgroup-specific artifacts.

ranking.rationale: Prior inpatient utilization is one of the most stable and strongest indicators of future readmission risk.
Recent emergency visit history robustly captures instability and acute care dependence across domains.
Length of stay is a strong cross-domain proxy for severity and complexity of the index admission.
Total medications administered reflects treatment complexity and comorbidity burden.
More diagnoses generally indicates higher multimorbidity and persistent readmission risk.
Prior outpatient utilization captures chronic disease burden and healthcare engagement.
Number of lab procedures is a broad severity and workup intensity signal.
Discharge disposition strongly relates to post-discharge support needs and near-term return risk, though somewhat practice-dependent.
Insulin dose escalation suggests poor glycemic control during admission and meaningful clinical instability.
Insulin dose reduction still carries direct treatment-state information relevant to readmission.
Being maintained on insulin indicates substantial diabetes management intensity.
Absence of insulin use is informative about treatment regimen and disease state.
Any medication change is a compact marker of active management and instability.
Presence of diabetes medication is clinically meaningful and broadly portable.
No diabetes medication also informs disease management intensity and care pathway.
Elevated HbA1c category is a direct, semantically stable marker of poor chronic glucose control.
Higher HbA1c category remains strongly predictive of uncontrolled diabetes and future risk.
Normal HbA1c provides useful contrast on chronic glycemic control.
Elevated serum glucose is an acute physiologic severity signal likely to generalize.
Very high serum glucose is a strong marker of acute metabolic instability.
Normal serum glucose helps distinguish lower-risk metabolic status.
Admission type captures urgency and acuity with moderate robustness across hospitals.
Procedure count reflects encounter complexity, though somewhat influenced by local practice.
Primary heart failure diagnosis is a classic high-readmission condition across settings.
Secondary heart failure diagnosis also signals substantial chronic disease burden.
Additional heart failure diagnosis further captures multimorbidity linked to readmission.
Acute myocardial infarction as primary diagnosis indicates serious cardiovascular illness with persistent risk.
Coronary atherosclerotic disease is a durable predictor of recurrent utilization.
Renal failure as primary diagnosis strongly predicts recurrent hospitalization.
Renal failure as secondary diagnosis is similarly important for chronic instability.
Urinary tract infection as secondary diagnosis often marks frailty and recurrent acute care use.
Fluid and electrolyte disorders are strong severity markers that generalize well.
Secondary fluid and electrolyte disorders indicate instability and complexity.
Additional fluid and electrolyte disorder burden remains clinically meaningful.
Hypertension as a secondary diagnosis contributes to chronic cardiometabolic burden.
Hypertension in additional diagnoses adds stable comorbidity information.
Secondary diabetes diagnosis is directly relevant to disease burden and complications.
Additional diabetes diagnosis contributes to overall diabetic complexity.
Primary diabetes diagnosis category is clinically relevant to readmission risk.
Another primary diabetes diagnosis subtype remains semantically predictive.
Primary diabetes complication subtype also reflects disease severity.
Secondary diabetes complication subtype adds useful chronic disease detail.
Another secondary diabetes subtype remains relevant to diabetic burden.
Additional diabetes complication subtype contributes stable risk information.
Additional secondary diabetes subtype is still clinically meaningful.
Older age is a robust predictor of frailty and readmission.
Age 70-80 strongly tracks chronic illness burden and vulnerability.
Age 80-90 is highly informative for frailty-related readmission risk.
Age 50-60 remains predictive through accumulated chronic disease burden.
Very advanced age is important, though sample size may be smaller.
Middle age still carries useful baseline risk information.
Age 30-40 is less predictive but still part of stable patient context.
Age 20-30 is usually lower risk yet semantically valid.
Metformin nonuse helps characterize treatment intensity and disease phenotype.
Stable metformin use is a portable marker of outpatient diabetes management.
Metformin escalation may indicate active glycemic management.
Glimepiride nonuse contributes regimen information with some clinical relevance.
Stable glimepiride use reflects diabetes treatment pattern.

Stable glipizide use carries moderate treatment-state information.

Pioglitazone nonuse contributes modest regimen information.
